channel.title: Tianlun's Picks
channel.description: AI-curated episodes on AI in healthcare operations and AI-services business models.
channel.itunes:author: Podcast Curator

item.title: [Vanguards of Healthcare] Abridge Moving AI From Scribing to Clinical Workflows
item.description:
WHY YOU: Abridge's co-founder/CTO (Zack Lipton) on the thesis every AI-RCM and EHR vendor you watch is now copying: that the scribe is a wedge, not the product, and that the money is in one platform that steers documentation, billing/coding and care decisions in real time at the point of care — which is exactly the layer that decides whether a stand-alone billing or coding vendor keeps its seat. Also how a research-heavy team turned that into the category leader. Caveats: March 2026 (8 months old; classic slot), Bloomberg Intelligence analyst host, no pricing or contract figures in the notes; 52 minutes.
Abridge co-founder and CTO Zack Lipton joins Bloomberg Intelligence healthcare analyst Jonathan Palmer to discuss how the company grew from a research-heavy idea into a leader in health care AI. He argues that point solutions are limited and that the future is a unified platform that guides documentation, billing and care decisions in real time at the point of care — not just a better digital scribe.

item.title: [Vanguards of Healthcare] Athenahealth's Strategic Reset, Push for Speed in Ambulatory Care
item.description:
WHY YOU: The CEO of the EHR+RCM incumbent that most of your practices run on (Bob Segert) on the business decisions behind it: cutting the weak bets to focus on ambulatory care and a single cloud platform (athenaOne), the open-platform strategy that decides which third-party AI billing/front-office tools get in, the AI push, and physician economics — i.e. what an EHR vendor thinks it is selling to a practice and what it will let others sell alongside it. Pairs with the Paul Brient (athenahealth CPO/COO) episode from Nov 21. Caveats: April 2026 (8 months old; classic slot), analyst host, no pricing mechanics in the notes; second item from this show in the batch because nothing else cleared the bar; 51 minutes.
Bob Segert, CEO of Athenahealth, joins Bloomberg Intelligence healthcare analyst Jonathan Palmer to describe the company's strategic reset — cutting weaker bets and focusing on ambulatory care and the cloud-native athenaOne platform — along with its AI push, an open-platform strategy, and physician economics.

item.title: [Vanguards of Healthcare] Smarter Technologies' Blueprint for AI-Driven Revenue Cycle Management
item.description:
WHY YOU: The CEO of the company that merged SmarterDx, Thoughtful AI and Access Healthcare into one AI-plus-BPO revenue-cycle operator — the “AI-native incumbent” you compete against and get compared to — on how he splits revenue cycle into two problems (producing an accurate claim, then the many steps to actually get paid), where AI works as a first pass under human supervision and where it does not, how better RCM workflow shows up in a hospital's thin operating margin, and why a PE firm (New Mountain) assembled the company this way. Caveats: January 2026 (10 months old; classic slot), Bloomberg Intelligence analyst host rather than an operator host, no pricing figures in the notes; 53 minutes.
Dr. Michael Gao, CEO of Smarter Technologies (formerly co-founder and CEO of SmarterDx), joins Bloomberg Intelligence healthcare analyst Jonathan Palmer to discuss how AI is changing hospital revenue cycle management. He frames revenue cycle as two problems: producing an accurate charge record, then the many steps needed to get paid. They cover Smarter's approach to clinical intelligence and automation, why AI works best as a first pass with human supervision, how smarter RCM workflows can lift margins for hospitals operating on very thin economics, Smarter's formation by New Mountain Capital from three predecessor companies, and Gao's mission to reduce the trillion-dollar burden of health care administration.

item.title: [Vanguards of Healthcare] Innovaccer's Bet on the Data Layer Powering Autonomous Healthcare
item.description:
WHY YOU: A scaled healthcare-AI vendor's CEO (Abhinav Shashank) on the business-model question behind “autonomous healthcare”: why he thinks the data layer, not the model, decides whether AI can take administrative waste out of a health system, how a company covering ~80 million patient lives thinks about getting to $1B ARR, and his own warning about what badly designed automation does inside a provider organisation. Caveats: Aug 13 (3.5 months), analyst host, no pricing mechanics in the notes; 50 minutes.
Innovaccer co-founder and CEO Abhinav Shashank joins Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Jonathan Palmer. He argues that fixing healthcare's fragmented data is the foundation for AI, and that “autonomous healthcare” could cut administrative waste. The company now covers about 80 million patient lives and is targeting $1 billion in annual recurring revenue. The conversation also covers the risks of poorly designed automation in healthcare.

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Health plans landed on the CEO's desk | Owen Tripp, Included Health [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: The payer side of the AI-coding arms race you work inside: Included Health's CEO on the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association finding that AI-assisted coding is driving a claims-cost spike (41:40), the utilization backlash insurers are preparing (45:12) and the tools employers are reaching for (47:25) — plus why health-plan decisions moved from benefits teams to CFOs who want predictable pricing (24:14), and his claim that providers care more about getting paid fast than about a carrier's brand. Wildcard: most of the hour is health-plan strategy; journalist host; 59 minutes, published Nov 24.
Christina Farr talks with Owen Tripp, co-founder and CEO of Included Health, about the company's move into health plans after acquiring Firefly Health, and why large employers may finally be ready to leave the big carriers. Tripp argues health-plan decisions have shifted from benefits teams to CFOs and CEOs, that providers care more about getting paid quickly than about a carrier's brand, and discusses the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association report on AI-assisted coding and what insurers may do next. Timestamps: (01:21) Meet Owen Tripp; (02:30) Why buy Firefly; (05:10) Two plan models; (08:33) Digital health evolution; (11:42) Member-first strategy; (16:22) Mistrust in health plans; (18:51) Employers ready to switch; (24:14) CFO predictable pricing; (31:15) Defined contribution limits; (35:57) Network access myth; (41:40) Blues AI cost spike; (45:12) AI utilization backlash; (47:25) Employer response tools; (50:47) Staying in the fight.

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Systems of record vs. systems of action: the future of the EHR | Paul Brient, athenahealth
item.description:
WHY YOU: The EHR incumbent's product and operations chief on the system you sell into and around: why a closed EHR risks becoming a database under other companies' AI agents (14:10), why agents get blocked from booking care (17:21), what happens when the clinical and financial sides don't talk (24:58), payers, zero-sum games and the revenue cycle (26:10), the Humana prior-authorization deal and what it changes (28:53), gold carding and provider report cards (32:02), and why athenahealth is exploring open-weight models (44:29). Caveats: journalist host, no pricing or margin figures in the notes; 58 minutes, published Nov 21.
Chrissy Farr talks with Paul Brient, Chief Product and Operations Officer at athenahealth, about the AI-native EHR and why closed systems risk becoming a database underneath other companies' AI agents. They cover whether leadership cares more about billing or patient care, meaningful use and what AI changes about interoperability, why AI agents get blocked from booking healthcare, letting patients connect their records to Claude, when the clinical and financial sides don't talk, payers and the revenue cycle, the Humana prior authorization deal, gold carding and provider report cards, open notes, why athenahealth is exploring open-weight models, and how engineering jobs are changing. Timestamps: (0:00) Intro; (1:37) Welcome Paul Brient; (2:44) athenahealth started as a chain of OB-GYN clinics; (4:08) Disruptor, incumbent, or leader?; (6:10) Who athenahealth serves today; (7:55) Does leadership care more about billing or patient care?; (9:56) Meaningful use, interoperability, and what AI changes; (13:07) Will AI cement faxes as healthcare's interoperability?; (14:10) Systems of record vs. systems of action: the AI-native EHR; (17:21) Why AI agents get blocked from booking healthcare; (21:06) Letting patients connect their records to Claude; (22:43) What about care that happens outside athenahealth?; (24:58) When the clinical and financial sides don't talk; (26:10) Payers, zero-sum games, and the revenue cycle; (28:53) The Humana prior authorization deal; (32:02) Gold carding and provider report cards; (35:12) Open notes and empowered patients; (39:03) Paul's path: billing software at 15 and the first electronic claim in Florida; (42:38) What physician workflow will look like in 20 years; (44:29) Why athenahealth is exploring open-weight models; (47:10) The AI story: reimagining how healthcare software gets built; (49:36) 3,000 engineers on call and 1,000 ideas at Thrive; (52:00) How engineering jobs are changing; (54:26) Practical advice: learn to manage your agents; (56:34) Wrap-up.

item.title: [Day1Global生而全球] E78. AI 应用的四层模型：卖算力、卖能力、卖入口、卖结果 ft. EvoseAI Bingo [中文]
item.description:
WHY YOU: A Mandarin framework for the pricing question you keep circling: an AI-agent founder back from 20 days inside US vertical-AI companies (legal, insurance, customer service) lays out four ways AI apps charge: selling compute, capability, an entry point, or outcomes (18:36), with the key observation that selling outcomes moves the spend from the IT budget to the labour budget (00:00), how vertical AI firms charge per point solution and why some are buying law firms (12:02), why the last 20% in production is the hard part (15:34), and why PMF cannot be outsourced to local sales hires when entering the US (51:00). Caveats: non-operator hosts and a framework rather than a P&L; published mid-June, five months old; 64 minutes.
Day1Global 主播 Star 和 Ruby 对谈 evose.ai 联合创始人 Bingo，他刚结束约 20 天的美国 AI / ToB 公司走访（Linkloud 加速器、SaaStr，以及 NVIDIA、Google、Foxit、Exa 和法律、保险、客服等垂直 AI 公司）。核心问题：AI 软件公司到底怎么赚钱。提出 AI 应用的四层商业模型：卖算力、卖能力、卖入口、卖结果；讨论美国创业公司切小能力与中国创始人包揽全企业需求的差异、中美 ToB 付费、资本市场和退出的差别、Agent 与 Agent 协作（一个营销 campaign 从四天压缩到一两个小时）、组织向 builder 和 reviewer 重组，以及中国 AI 公司进入美国市场的建议。时间线：00:00 精彩片段：卖结果让预算从 IT 预算转向人力预算；01:05 嘉宾介绍与 20 天硅谷 AI/ToB 之旅；03:42 硅谷走访：NVIDIA 与 Google 的反差，Foxit、Exa 与美国退出路径；12:02 垂直 AI 与资本杠杆：法律、保险、客服 AI 按单点能力收费，AI 公司收购律所；15:34 中美创始人的信息差，生产环境最后 20% 最难；18:36 四层模型：算力、能力、入口、结果；23:11 四层模型内的中美差异；30:39 从问答到干活：Evose 的 Agent 协作与通用大模型的区别；37:41 未来组织：builder 与 reviewer 取代部门和岗位；40:06 为什么 pivot 在硅谷是时髦词，Chief Storyteller；51:00 中国 AI 公司如何进入美国市场，PMF 不能外包给本地销售；59:51 一年后回看：infra 和结果层的泡沫，入口层的长期价值。

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Inside the Complexity of U.S. Healthcare: Kumar Shwetabh of Access Healthcare
item.description:
WHY YOU: The incumbent you compete with, in his own words: the Group President and Global COO of Access Healthcare, one of the big offshore RCM outsourcers, on where the money actually gets stuck. The claim path from coding to clearinghouse to payer and why providers wait weeks or months to be paid (7:03, 8:30), why clinical and financial systems still don't talk (12:01), why AI agents built on incomplete data fall short (14:30), automating prior auth (16:30), payers and providers now blocking each other's bots (19:40), the rise in denials and appeals and how to prevent them (22:15, 24:03), why payers don't publish their rules (27:00), the case for gold carding (30:15), and the candid part for a BPO executive: which revenue-cycle jobs disappear and which stay (38:04, 44:15). Caveats: a journalist host rather than an operator, and no pricing or margin figures in the notes; 54 minutes, published Nov 18.
Chrissy Farr talks with Kumar Shwetabh, Group President and Global COO of Access Healthcare, a veteran of more than two decades in US healthcare billing who founded Pacific BPO. They cover why providers wait weeks or months to get paid, how a claim moves from coding to clearinghouse to payer, and why AI agents built on incomplete data fall short. The conversation also covers automating prior authorization, payers and providers blocking each other's bots, the growth in denials and appeals, the case for gold carding, and his view that the revenue cycle workforce will shrink. Timestamps: (0:00) Intro; (2:04) Meet Kumar; (3:54) First impressions of US healthcare; (5:56) Cash pay, concierge medicine, specialist bottleneck; (7:03) Why providers wait months to get paid; (8:30) How a claim works; (12:01) Clinical and financial sides don't talk; (14:30) Can AI agents work on incomplete data; (16:30) Automating prior authorization; (19:40) Payers and providers blocking each other's bots; (22:15) More denials and appeals; (24:03) Preventing denials; (27:00) Why payers don't publish the rules; (30:15) The case for gold carding; (34:00) Why physicians avoid the revenue cycle; (38:04) AI and administrative jobs; (44:15) Which jobs stay; (46:15) Winners and losers in the AI era; (49:45) Would Kumar want his kids in this industry; (52:00) Wrap-up.

item.title: [Practical AI in Healthcare] S2E1 - Raihan Faroqui, MD: The Doctor at the Front Desk, AI on the Line
item.description:
WHY YOU: The closest thing found this run to the healthcare-AI GTM operator episode you asked for: Confido Health's VP of Partnerships (an internist turned front-office seller) on putting AI voice agents on the phone lines of about 1,500 outpatient sites for scheduling, refills, insurance checks and billing questions, in twenty languages. What you learn: the economics of an unanswered call as the sales wedge, why the deployment motion looks more like consulting than software (no migration, but heavy configuration per practice), how they define and measure agent failure with the customer, and the disclosure question (the agents don't tell patients they are AI). Hosts are two sceptical clinician-informaticists, not a vendor. Caveats: Sep 6 (about 11 weeks old), no pricing or contract numbers in the notes, a conference promo in the first minutes, and the show's RSS was unreadable this run so the audio URL comes from the show's Anchor host via a directory page.
Raihan Faroqui trained in internal medicine, then moved into venture-backed startups and, as he puts it, to the front desk. As VP of Partnerships at Confido Health he puts AI agents on the phone lines of roughly 1,500 outpatient practice sites, handling appointments, refills, insurance checks and billing questions in twenty languages. His argument is that healthcare's core problem has been a system-of-record problem rather than a software problem, and that agents are the first tool that does not require a migration. The episode covers the economics of an unanswered phone call, why the deployment model looks more like consulting than software, how the company defines and measures agent failure, and why these agents do not tell patients they are agents. Hosts: Steven Labkoff, MD and Leon Rozenblit.

item.title: [AI to ROI] The AI Agent Outcome-Based Pricing Journey - with Kunal Agarwal, CFO Gorgias
item.description:
WHY YOU: The CFO's view of per-outcome pricing, which is the piece the Sierra and Intercom episodes left out: Gorgias charges per AI resolution, so the finance side has to defend gross margins that run below classic SaaS, track LLM cost per interaction (third-party episode notes put inference at roughly 55 to 60% of the fully loaded cost of an AI interaction), decide what counts as a resolution versus a deflection, and work out attribution when a shopping agent influences a sale. It also covers why they re-architected the help desk around agents instead of bolting AI on, and how the pricing was iterated with customers. Caveats: May 2026, so near the six-month line; e-commerce support, not healthcare; 33 minutes; the host runs a SaaS benchmarking firm. Rough markers from third-party notes, not the show notes: why outcome pricing 12:10, pricing iteration 15:28, gross margin and inference cost 17:29, LLM share of COGS 23:13.
Ray Rike talks with Kunal Agarwal, CFO of Gorgias, the customer-experience platform for Shopify merchants, about building and pricing its AI agent product. Gorgias rebuilt its platform around AI agents rather than adding AI to the existing help desk, starting with email support in mid-2024, and chose full AI resolution rate over deflection rate as its north-star metric. It prices per resolution, so it is paid only when the agent delivers a measurable outcome. Kunal explains why AI-agent gross margins sit below traditional SaaS margins, how Gorgias tracks LLM cost per interaction under CFO-led governance, the attribution problem for its shopping assistant, and why finance should own AI ROI measurement.

item.title: [Orbit, an Hg podcast] Lovable from zero to $400m in 15 months with CRO, Ryan Meadows
item.description:
WHY YOU: Another CRO walking through a pricing shift with numbers, the Legora-CRO format you asked for more of: Lovable moved its enterprise pricing from per-seat to consumption, took the short-term revenue hit, and watched one customer go from 200 product managers on seats to 8,500 active builders in two months; the three-stage enterprise adoption model (everyone prototypes, useful prototypes get hardened into load-bearing apps, then core workflows get rebuilt) is in effect the pilot-to-rollout design for a usage-priced product; and the sales team runs on an AI command centre, live-call assistant and in-house CPQ built on the product itself. About $400M ARR with roughly 150 people. Caveats: a short 28 minutes, hosted by Hg (a software PE firm), no margin or contract-size figures, August 2026, and Lovable is a coding product rather than an AI services company.
Released the week Lovable's valuation doubled to $13.3 billion, this episode has Hg's Tim Harrison in conversation with Ryan Meadows, Lovable's Chief Revenue Officer, who joined as a customer first. He covers reaching about $400 million in ARR in roughly 15 months with around 150 people, building a company without legacy tools, and a three-stage model for enterprise AI transformation: get everyone prototyping, harden useful prototypes into load-bearing applications, then rebuild core workflows from first principles. They also discuss Lovable's switch from seat-based to consumption-based enterprise pricing and the customer that went from 200 product managers to 8,500 active builders in two months, how Lovable runs its own go-to-market on its platform, and why most non-technical employees have still not built anything with AI.

item.title: [The GTMnow Podcast] How Sierra Went From $0 to $400M ARR in 2.5 Years | Reggie Marable (Chief Customer Officer, Sierra)
item.description:
WHY YOU: The Sierra side of the Legora-CRO episode you asked for more of: Sierra's first sales hire (employee 23, ex-Salesforce/Slack) on how outcome-based pricing actually operates, charging only when the agent resolves a case with no human and nothing when it escalates or the customer calls back (6:14, 8:22); the selling motion of a demo, then a paid one-to-four-month proof of concept where a dedicated team builds the agent, tests it on simulated traffic and ramps live traffic from 5% while forward-deployed engineers stay on the account (17:07); how you track pipeline when revenue is per outcome (28:37); sales, product and engineering organised by industry, healthcare among them (20:55); the curve from zero long-term contracts at the February 2024 stealth exit to $20M in the launch year, then $100M to $200M in six months and $200M to $400M in five, with $150M added in Q3 alone (14:21, 22:45); and the Elite Eight, eight senior leaders hired first and asked to carry a quota again (32:28). Caveats: Zero sponsor read at 16:24, host is GTMfund-affiliated, no margin or contract-size figures.
Sierra passed $400M in ARR, adding $150M in Q3 alone, after coming out of stealth in February 2024 with no long-term contracts. Reggie Marable, Chief Customer Officer and Sierra's first sales hire, covers his move from Salesforce and Slack, his bet on founders Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor, outcome-based pricing (Sierra is paid when its AI agents resolve an issue), the paid proof-of-concept plus forward-deployed-engineering motion, building his first sales team, and advice for founders making their first sales hire. Chapters: 0:56 the $400M milestone; 2:28 joining as employee 23; 6:14 what Sierra does and how outcome-based pricing works; 8:22 why outcome pricing was a bold 2024 bet; 9:46 board cadence; 10:49 founder-to-first-sales-hire transition; 12:23 scaling selling past 1,200 employees; 13:06 Head of Sales to Chief Customer Officer; 14:21 pre-revenue to $20M in the launch year; 16:24 sponsor break; 17:07 paid POC and forward-deployed engineering; 19:59 scale, voice, innovation; 20:55 organising go-to-market by industry; 22:14 key industries and government; 22:45 growth curve from $100M to $200M to $400M; 26:09 what he looks for in sellers; 27:36 hiring by consensus; 28:37 tracking pipeline under outcome-based pricing; 30:21 enterprise AI selling, unlocks and mistakes; 32:28 the Elite Eight framework for first sales hires; 33:29 leadership lessons; 34:48 underrated GTM advice; 36:49 the future of customer-service jobs and AI architects.

item.title: [42章经] 复盘 2C 和 2B Agent 发展脉络｜对谈 Afk.surf 创始人嘉琛 [中文]
item.description:
WHY YOU: A Mandarin founder on the B2B-agent business he is actually running, with the candour you weighted up after Liblib: why AFFiNE, his open-source knowledge-base product, was popular but hard to monetise (01:49); how a To-B governing agent that learns and takes over enterprise workflows won its first large customers (18:29) and the shared context an enterprise has to supply before an agent can act for it (20:52); whether LangChain/Dify/n8n-style tooling is already obsolete (26:11); and how an application company that trains private models for its clients thinks about cost and operations (33:32). It also places AI-services pricing in the 2C-vs-2B agent split you keep seeing (05:43, 13:41). Caveats: no pricing or revenue figures in the notes, and the host is a VC; the operator content is the second half.
42章经 host 曲凯 continues the show's Personal Agent and RLaaS threads with 贺嘉琛, founder of Afk.surf, who applies personal-agent ideas to B2B and trains private models for enterprises. He left a deep-learning and astrophysics PhD in 2020 to start up, built AFFiNE (an open-source document collaboration and knowledge-base product), helped incubate VoidZero with 尤雨溪 (later acquired by Cloudflare), and now runs Afk.surf, a To-B governing agent meant to learn and take over enterprise workflows while aligning with an organisation's business, working styles and preferences; the notes say it already has several large customers. Timestamps: 01:49 why AFFiNE was popular and why it was hard to commercialise; 05:43 from 2026 agents stop behaving like traditional software; 08:19 recent shifts in agent product forms; 09:50 review of personal-agent development; 10:43 2026 as the year of the most buzzwords; 13:41 whether To-C personal agents remain a platform opportunity and whether To-B is different; 18:29 how Afk won large customers; 20:52 the shared understanding enterprise collaboration needs; 26:11 whether LangChain, Dify and n8n are outdated; 33:32 how an app company that trains its own models thinks and operates; 40:02 whether AI could replace rule-based logic end to end; 42:34 whether the timing is right for AI games; 44:58 recruiting from the AFFiNE network.

item.title: [The Heart of Healthcare] Big Changes Are Underway for Medicare | CMS Chief AI & Technology Officer, Jacob Shiff [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: The payer-side answer to who pays for AI in care delivery, from someone who used to sell into it: the CMS Innovation Center's AI and technology lead co-founded Anomaly (the claims-accuracy startup) and worked at Flatiron before this job. He explains why fee-for-service rules make AI add billable services rather than remove cost, how the ACCESS model pays for measured improvement in patient health instead, what that changes for startups selling AI-enabled chronic-condition care, the CMS/FDA pathways being built for AI-delivered treatment (AI mental-health care included), and whether any of it survives a change of administration. Caveats: policy rather than operator numbers, Bessemer-hosted, 29 minutes, no timestamps; a wildcard because it is the reimbursement logic behind your buyers' budgets, not a GTM story.
Steve Kraus talks with Jacob Shiff, Chief AI and Technology Officer at the CMS Innovation Center, about how Medicare's payment policies could decide whether AI makes healthcare more or less expensive. They discuss why traditional payment models drive up the cost of new technology, how the ACCESS model pays for measurable improvements in patient health rather than additional billable services, what outcomes-based care would need to work at scale, what the model means for healthcare startups and for clinicians treating chronic conditions, how CMS and the FDA are creating pathways for AI-powered treatments including AI-delivered mental-health care, and whether these reforms can survive changes in administration. Before CMS, Jacob co-founded Anomaly (Series B, about $20M raised) and worked at Redesign Health, Flatiron Health and Google.

item.title: [The a16z Show] How Enterprise AI Really Gets Deployed
item.description:
WHY YOU: The Sierra-peer founder interview held since the 11-09 run; the a16z feed finally came back readable. Decagon's co-founders on the mechanics of getting AI customer-support, sales and operations agents live inside large enterprises: forward-deployed engineering as the deployment model and what of it stays, enterprise sales and rollout planning, latency/evaluation/fine-tuning as production constraints, and the margin lever of moving most inference to open-source models. A third-party summary of the episode (not the show notes) adds the points that make it worth your time: the CEO spending most of his time selling, Decagon's glass-box positioning against Sierra's FDE-heavy black box, and a customer going from a few support journeys a year on Sierra to several a month. Caveats: a16z-hosted (an investor), no pricing, ARR or margin figures in the notes, 3.5 months old, 80 minutes. Use it as the comparison point for how services-as-software companies scope a deployment and what they refuse to productize.
Sarah Wang and Kimberly Tan talk with Decagon co-founders Jesse Zhang and Ashwin Sreenivas about enterprise AI agents: why Decagon has moved most of its inference to open-source models, how it helps large companies take AI into production, its agents for customer support, sales and operational workflows, and how latency, evaluation and fine-tuning shape production systems. The conversation also covers forward-deployed engineering, enterprise sales, AI's effect on jobs, and why application companies can thrive alongside the foundation-model labs.

item.title: [The a16z Show] AI for America's Small Businesses | Lassie
item.description:
WHY YOU: The closest thing this run to a practice-side RCM operator with numbers. Lassie sells AI agents that read insurance claims, reconcile payments, post to the ledger and flag underpayments, denials and missing claims for small dental practices, which is the back office you sell into. From a16z's own write-ups and a third-party summary of the episode: 700+ practices in 49 states and $10M+ annualized revenue at the June 2026 Series A; the first agent priced at five figures per practice per year against roughly 30 hours a month of admin labor it replaces; a 98% automation rate with a >95% bar before a module ships; about 70% of practices still paid by paper check; and a GTM built around dentists being absent from LinkedIn and Apollo (licensing data, provider directories, office-manager job postings as intent signals, study clubs and state dental associations as referral channels), with messaging about hours of labor you cannot hire rather than AI. The candid bits: staff often prefer paper, which is why earlier software stalled, and self-serve onboarding is still months away. Caveats: a16z-hosted and a16z-led round, so a friendly interview; no timestamps; 3.5 months old; the second a16z item in this batch because nothing from another show cleared the bar.
Alex Rampell and Olivia Moore speak with Lassie co-founders Steijn Pelle and Frédéric Renken about bringing AI to small businesses. Inspired by time spent inside dental practices, they set out to automate administrative work such as billing, insurance claims and patient payments. The conversation covers AI agents, onboarding AI into real businesses, healthcare administration as an automation opportunity, product design, go-to-market strategy, and building AI systems that run reliably in complex environments.

item.title: [The GTMnow Podcast] Inside Exa's Run to $100M ARR: Building Google for AI Agents | Marcus Holm (CRO, Exa) [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Same show and format as the Legora-CRO episode you liked, but for a consumption-priced AI company. A CRO (ex-LaunchDarkly president) on the part of usage-based pricing that most AI-services pricing talk skips: how to structure rep compensation when revenue is consumption rather than seats (15:29), why consumption means selling continuously after signature (17:01), moving customers from pay-as-you-go to enterprise contracts (18:36), economic-buyer alignment (36:05) and teaching multithreading (38:20), plus hiring, ramping and letting go of reps (24:42 to 29:40). Wildcard because Exa sells search infrastructure to developers, not services, and the $100M ARR headline is the hook rather than the lesson. Held since 10-27. Sponsor read (Nooks) at 14:59.
Exa recently crossed $100M ARR after growing roughly 10x a year for nearly three years. CRO Marcus Holm, formerly president at LaunchDarkly, explains how the company is building search for AI agents, why co-founder Will's prediction that agents would search more than humans in 2026 has come true, and what that means for SEO, ads and salespeople. He also covers selling to developers, designing consumption-based compensation, aligning executive buyers, and hiring and ramping reps. item.title: [BUILDERS] Why winning the C-suite is not enough in healthcare AI | James Bates
item.description:
WHY YOU: A 21-minute practice-side GTM brief from the CEO of AdviNow Medical, which sells billing, claims and compliance automation to small and mid-size practices, i.e. the buyer you sell to. The claims to test against your own motion: a stopwatch-and-spreadsheet Six Sigma analysis that found physicians spending about 70% of their time on billing and compliance rather than medicine; practices moving from low-single-digit to roughly 35% profitability after onboarding (his figure, unverified); growth that is 100% referral-driven because the profitability change sells itself; and the title lesson that a CEO signing over the CTO's objection creates a saboteur, so the champion below the C-suite has to be won before the signature. Caveats: an agency-produced founder show with a sponsor read, no pricing or ARR, and the profitability number is vendor talk. Held from the 11-09 run; BUILDERS' second item in two batches.
AdviNow Medical automates the non-physical work of a medical practice with four AI systems covering diagnostic reasoning, treatment planning, billing and claims, and legal and compliance review. CEO James Bates came into healthcare intending to buy practices and changed course after a stopwatch-and-spreadsheet lean analysis of how physicians actually spend their day, which put roughly 70% of their time on billing and compliance. Topics: the practice evaluations, sequencing which work to automate first, identifying the intelligence a workflow needs before building it, choosing the first customer, profitability-driven referral growth, change management inside practices, why winning the CEO is not enough if the people below resist, and the AI roll-up thesis. Formerly published as Category Visionaries (Front Lines Media); ends with a sponsor credit for the Front Lines studio.

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Rounds: Take the Money and R1, Megan Scheffel, Dan Bise, and Jeremy Friese
item.description:
WHY YOU: The acquirer's side of AI-RCM M&A. R1, one of the largest outsourced revenue-cycle operators and freshly taken private by CD&R and TowerBrook, explains through its EVP of strategy why it bought Phare Health and Humata Health and how Humata's prior-authorization platform is meant to cut downstream payer denials; then Humata founder Jeremy Friese says what set R1 apart from the other bidders and why he sold rather than kept building. Useful for your own map of who ends up owning prior auth and denials work, and what a strategic buyer pays for. Caveats: a Rounds episode, so it opens with headlines (Oura's S-1, SVB's exits report) before the interviews; sponsored by SVB, whose healthcare head is one of the three guests; no timestamps; six weeks old. Held since the 10-26 run; Lifers' fourth item in this feed.
Episode 5 of Rounds. Christina Farr and healthcare analyst Stephanie Davis open with the week's headlines, including Oura's S-1 (about $1.4B in revenue) and a former Anthropic researcher's warning to the BBC, then bring in three guests. Megan Scheffel, head of life science and healthcare at SVB, walks through SVB's Healthcare Investments and Exits report: fewer specialised funds behind the fundraising slowdown, deal volume at a multi-year low with total dollars steady, investors favouring proven commercial viability, and the split between a record biopharma M&A year and a healthtech market with strong IPO performance but few listings. Dan Bise, EVP of strategy and corporate development at R1, explains the thesis behind CD&R and TowerBrook's take-private, R1's shift to an AI-native, technology-first approach to revenue-cycle automation, the acquisitions of Phare Health and Humata Health, and how Humata's prior authorization platform reduces downstream payer denials. Jeremy Friese, founder and CEO of Humata Health, explains what set R1 apart from other potential acquirers and why he chose to sell. Sponsored by Silicon Valley Bank.

item.title: [晚点聊 LateTalk] 186: Anthropic招股书丨"银行也有百亿预算"，与Fusion Fund张璐聊大企业在想什么 [中文] [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: The demand side of AI-services pricing, in Mandarin: Fusion Fund's 张璐, drawing on a CTO/CIO network at 40-plus large companies, on what enterprise buyers actually budget for AI, whether they have seen returns yet, why reworking a workflow takes years rather than quarters, and where back-office agents in regulated industries such as finance, legal and healthcare are getting money (42:00, 45:29). Pricing and growth at 08:05. Investor-side and framed around the Anthropic S-1 rather than an operator with numbers, hence the wildcard: held for three runs as the Mandarin fallback for a thin batch, and this batch is thin.
晚点聊主播程曼祺对话 Fusion Fund 联合创始合伙人张璐。她在硅谷投资 B2B 科技 11 年，维护着一个覆盖 40 多家全球大公司 CTO、CIO 的 CXO 网络。本期聚焦大企业对 AI 和 token 的真实需求：客户在想什么、在用什么场景、回报是否已经兑现、新的增长出现在哪里。章节：Anthropic 从非共识押注走向主流（估值、收入增速、员工锁定设计、早期投资人与竞争格局）；08:05 定价与增长；coding 之外：Anthropic 能否成为企业 agent 平台、财富 500 强为何把 AI 列为优先事项、改造工作流为何以年计；29:11 是否会有第二个 coding 量级的突破；42:00 金融、法律、医疗等行业的采用情况；45:29 强监管行业的后台 agent 创业机会，以及 AI for science 在药物研发中的应用；59:28 长期算力承诺的风险、中型公司转售 GPU、更清晰的监管对企业采用的作用。结论：需求是关键变量。

item.title: [A Product Market Fit Show] He had paying customers before he even incorporated, then hit $1M ARR in a year and raised a $19M Series A. | Rahul Shivkumar, Co-Founder of Assured
item.description:
WHY YOU: The healthcare version of the Legora CRO episode you asked for. Assured does AI credentialing and payer enrollment (the product side is already in your feed via Kanter); this is the sales motion, with numbers: two customers signed before the company was incorporated and four new logos in one week (02:21), starting at the front door of the revenue cycle (11:36), the ROI math and where it falls flat (21:28), $1M ARR in a year and how one small logo opens a whole specialty (30:25), six human BDRs at 150–200 calls a day and 8% pickup beating AI SDRs (34:27), and discovery-before-demo lifting close rate from 18% to 40% (48:20). Host Pablo Srugo is a VC, but the numbers are the founder's. Held since 11-06 for a missing audio URL; the buzzsprout feed exposed it this run.
Rahul ran a sleep clinic that lived on insurance paperwork, sold it, and built the tool he wished he had. Two customers signed before incorporation; $1M ARR within a year; a $19M Series A. The episode covers why the team chose six human BDRs over AI SDRs, how running discovery before demos raised the close rate, and why landing one small customer can open an entire medical specialty. Chapters: 00:00 Intro; 02:21 Four new customers in one week; 05:14 From Dawn Health to Assured; 11:36 Starting at the front door of revenue cycle; 18:00 Human in the loop, 100% accuracy; 21:28 The ROI math, and when it falls flat; 30:25 $1M ARR and the power of one logo; 34:27 Why human BDRs beat AI SDRs; 48:20 Discovery before the demo; 51:27 Getting stalled deals over the line.

item.title: [BUILDERS] How Arintra built a 100% pilot success rate by leading with ROI in autonomous medical coding | Nitesh Shroff
item.description:
WHY YOU: A 19-minute GTM brief from the CEO of an autonomous medical-coding company selling into hospitals: why a 6–8 month sales cycle counts as fast in this market, pilots run as the conversion path with value shown inside 2–3 months, the pilot metrics he closes on (5–8% compliant revenue uplift, 32% coding cost reduction, 64% faster collections), and how the same deal is pitched to the CFO (margin), the VP of Revenue Cycle (leverage and compliance) and the Director of Coding (Epic/Athena/NextGen integration). The wedge argument — enter through a workflow the hospital cannot skip, not a productivity pitch — is the one to test against your own front-office positioning. Caveats: April 2026 (just past the six-month window), an agency-produced B2B founder show with sponsor reads, and no pricing or ARR.
Medical coding is a mandatory workflow: no code, no claim, no payment. The US is not producing enough coders, payer complexity keeps growing and hospital margins are thin. Arintra CEO and co-founder Nitesh Shroff explains how the company wins deals in a slow, high-stakes market: a 6–8 month sales cycle, a 100% pilot success rate, and ROI that compounds across the revenue cycle. Topics: the $19,000 ER bill behind the company; how the coding shortage, payer complexity and margin pressure created an urgent buying motion; the metrics behind the pilot record (5–8% compliant revenue uplift, 32% cost reduction, 64% faster collections); persona messaging for the CFO, VP of Revenue Cycle and Director of Coding; expanding from autonomous coding into CDI, prior authorization and denial prevention; the 'document, charge, get paid' platform vision. Formerly published as Category Visionaries (Front Lines Media).

item.title: [十字路口Crossing] AI 下半场，不会只剩一个超级模型｜对谈 Kevin Ding：Pyromind 创始人/CEO [中文] [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: The FDE-economics question from a founder's side of the table, in Mandarin: a post-training-as-a-service (RLaaS) startup on why forward-deployed work is unavoidable at entry and how it declines (10:16), how to get industrial clients to calculate ROI (22:13), the three criteria for accepting an enterprise request (23:22), how two FDEs support a dozen-plus B2B clients and which work gets pulled into product (34:02), whether the company earns more or less as models need less training (38:20) and why AI ToB can make ROI legible where Chinese SaaS could not (40:58). Industrial RL rather than healthcare and no numbers in the notes, hence the wildcard; pairs with the Rolling AI FDE episode already in your feed.
Kevin Ding is founder and CEO of Pyromind, an RL-as-a-service company that recently closed an angel round (Hillhouse, Baidu Ventures, Banchi, Atypical). The show notes present AutoRL — an automated loop of training, rewards, feedback, deployment and data reflow — as the main bet, with use cases in industrial quality inspection, process-parameter optimisation, GUI agents and coding agents, and PyroDash, a hybrid architecture pairing a 4B worker model with a strong base model. Timestamps: 00:23 quick-fire (background, company stats); 01:55 why the endgame looks like a swarm of agents, not one super model; 03:44 why RSI mattered this year; 05:21 which half of the problem RLaaS solves; 08:32 selecting customers suited to AutoRL; 10:16 why FDE work is unavoidable at first and declines later; 22:13 helping industrial clients calculate ROI; 23:22 three criteria for accepting an enterprise request; 26:29 cost, efficiency and privacy trade-offs; 27:03 how PyroDash coordinates models; 29:23 problems harnesses cannot solve; 34:02 how two FDEs support a dozen-plus clients and what moves into product; 38:20 whether Pyromind earns more or less as models need less training; 40:58 why AI ToB can make ROI clear despite the difficulty of Chinese SaaS; 42:06 could cloud providers absorb Pyromind; 47:47 why demand will not consolidate into one base model.

item.title: [Sourcery] Commure Hits $7B Backed by GC, Sequoia, Morgan Stanley
item.description:
WHY YOU: The P&L of an AI-native RCM company from the CEO running the largest one: 85%+ of revenue-cycle work now completes with no human in the loop, ARR has doubled three years running across 500+ organizations and 3,000+ care sites, and he explains why point-solution AI vendors 'will be gone in three years', how General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund finances the health-system sales motion, and what the Augmedix and Summa Health deals were for. Sourcery's written companion to this episode adds the margin split (SaaS high-80s/90s vs full-cycle RCM high-60s in implementation, mid-70s at steady state) — the reference numbers for every contingency or percent-of-collections AI RCM pitch you evaluate. Held since the 10-29 extra batch; the anchor feed finally resolved this run. Host Molly O'Shea is a VC-adjacent interviewer, but this is the CEO talking numbers.
Tanay Tandon, co-founder and CEO of Commure, on the company's $70M raise at a $7B post-money valuation led by General Catalyst, with Sequoia, Morgan Stanley and Kirkland & Ellis participating; $750M raised to date. Commure runs inside 500+ healthcare organizations and 3,000+ care sites and completes 85%+ of revenue cycle work without a human in the loop. Founded when Tandon was 18 from a Stanford dorm; now 1,200 employees and ARR doubled three years running. Topics: General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund, why platforms beat point solutions, the Augmedix acquisition, the Summa Health partnership, and the path to an IPO. 57 minutes.

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Healthcare AI needs humans | Microsoft's Peter Lee & Seattle Children's Chris Longhurst
item.description:
WHY YOU: The buyer's-side answer to the question under every scribe and back-office pitch: a children's-hospital CEO and Microsoft's health-AI lead on why ambient scribes still lack a clean financial win (09:27), where the back-office cost curve actually bends (21:36), which admin jobs change and what skills replace them (23:12), the copilot-to-agent step (30:11) and the three Cs — competence, communication, character — that keep humans in the loop (36:25). Calibration for how a health-system buyer will score the ROI slide of any AI RCM or front-office vendor. Held since 10-26 for a missing enclosure; the megaphone feed finally gave it up this run. Journalist-hosted; a Granola ad read at 18:09, unrelated to the guests.
Christina Farr hosts Peter Lee (Microsoft) and Chris Longhurst (CEO, Seattle Children's) on where healthcare AI really stands versus the hype: why ambient scribes lack a clear financial win, Longhurst's prediction that within 3-5 years an AI-aided physician assistant could match top general pediatricians, the competence/communication/character test for keeping humans in the loop, and Lee's worry that AI gets used to dodge accountability. Timestamps: 00:00 Lead in; 00:28 Intro; 01:23 Massive moment; 04:01 ER reality; 06:12 Upskilling; 07:13 Tech CEOs; 09:27 Scribe costs; 13:43 Hierarchy; 15:23 Workforce; 18:09 Sponsor; 18:55 Training; 21:36 Back office; 23:12 Admin skills; 27:50 Self-driving; 30:11 Agents; 32:59 Clinical autonomy; 36:25 Humans in loop; 39:27 Accountability; 41:37 Frontier models; 46:35 Interoperability; 47:53 Wrap. item.title: [Raising Health] The AI-Native Health Plan | UnitedHealth Group's Dan Kueter [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: The payer side of prior auth and denials, from UnitedHealth Group's chief commercial officer: UnitedHealthcare's stated goal of eliminating 30% of prior authorizations and what a 'touchless' PA would look like, self-funded plans reaching smaller employers, how AI changes underwriting and distribution, and personal AI agents as a new front door that payers must meet. a16z-hosted (Julie Yoo, recorded at a16z BUILD) and polished, no pricing numbers, hence the wildcard — but 38 minutes to hear what the largest payer says it will stop asking for is worth it for anyone billing against it.
Can AI make healthcare cheaper? UnitedHealth Group Chief Commercial Officer Dan Kueter thinks it could within a single-digit number of years, once AI moves past automating administrative work to enabling new capabilities. Recorded at a16z BUILD with Julie Yoo, the conversation covers a major shift in employer-backed coverage, why self-funded plans are reaching smaller employers, how AI is reshaping underwriting, distribution and consumer navigation, UnitedHealthcare's goal of eliminating 30% of prior authorizations and what a touchless version could look like, and how personal AI agents could become a new entry point to healthcare that pushes insurers to meet people wherever they engage. 38 minutes.

item.title: [十字路口Crossing] OpenAI 和 Anthropic 共同看好的 FDE：AI 时代的新岗位出现，旧分工松动｜对谈 Rolling AI [中文]
item.description:

Listener comments dispute the firm's client count and scale, so treat the numbers as claims.
主播 Koji 对谈 Rolling AI 合伙人阿甘和刘开，聊 OpenAI 与 Anthropic 同日宣布的 FDE（前线部署工程师）岗位与企业 AI 落地的生意。01:08 快问快答：背景、公司、收入、利润、团队规模、过往经历；02:19 AI 是劳动力而非软件，FDE 像 HRBP 把'数字员工'放进企业，为何离开 BCG，MBB 在中国民企遇到的问题；08:22 第一个案例：乳企用 AI agent 服务约 600 万用户，营养师与目标用户之间约 200 倍的供给缺口，最难的是找到好的人类专家来训练 AI；19:58 FDE 要完成业务融合、知识治理、系统打通才能离场，好的 FDE 兼具问题诊断、人机协作和快速原型能力；25:09 SOP 意味着慢，总部从控制转向赋能，管理层级会被压缩；28:21 企业失败不是因为没用新技术——技术只占 AI 落地的不到三分之一；32:01 三种失败模式：CEO 期望不切实际、IT 主导而非业务主导、激励机制没有随技术改变；43:29 应届生能提供什么，如何判断商业 sense；46:49 实验室为何入场 FDE：数据与行业知识缺口是模型落地的主要障碍，ToB 本质是服务生意，JV 为何采用 PE 式结构；49:08 商业模式：FDE 公司更适合被 VC 持有而非被 VC 投资，一个行业只服务一家，未来是 Service as Software 还是 Result as a Service。约 55 分钟。

item.title: [42章经] 一个 AI 创始人的虚荣心、装，和愚昧之巅｜对谈 invoko.ai 创始人梦琪 [中文] [wildcard]

item.title: [Lenny's Podcast] Pricing your AI product: Lessons from 400+ companies and 50 unicorns | Madhavan Ramanujam
item.description:

The framework to judge every pricing story in your feed.
Madhavan Ramanujam (Simon-Kucher; Monetizing Innovation / Scaling Innovation) on pricing AI products. (04:30) Core thesis (09:20) Common traps (12:06) Beautifully simple pricing (15:00) Negotiations (27:35) How AI pricing is different (31:33) Handling POCs (38:58) Choosing the AI pricing model (43:13) Current trends (44:48) Outcome-based models (50:23) Packaging (53:40) Pricing axioms.

item.description:

Eoghan McCabe, founder and CEO of Intercom, on how the company went from stagnation to one of the leading AI customer-service businesses by betting everything on AI: the wartime reset, the Fin AI agent and outcome-based pricing, culture and leadership changes.

item.title: [Pear Healthcare Playbook] Lessons from Jeffery Liu, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Assort Health, on Fixing the Front Door of Healthcare with AI Agents
item.description:
WHY YOU: One of the fastest-growing AI front-office companies (specialty-specific voice agents for scheduling and triage), on what its first real deployments taught it and how it turns custom implementations per specialty into a platform. That's the scaling problem every 'we do the work' healthcare AI company hits.
Jeffery Liu, co-founder and co-CEO of Assort Health, on specialty-specific AI voice agents for patient access: how Assort started, why patient access is still hard to fix, lessons from early deployments, handling scheduling and triage complexity, scaling customized implementations into a platform, and AI patient navigation across voice and text.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Payer enrollment with Megan Struxness at Bridge
item.description:
WHY YOU: The provider-side plumbing you run every day, from the head of payer ops and RCM at Bridge: how payer contracting and enrollment actually work, superbills and out-of-network claims, the limits of eligibility checks, how Bridge offers guaranteed payment, and how it gets providers enrolled and billing in about 45 days. Directly comparable to Klarity's own provider onboarding.
Megan Struxness is Head of Payer Operations and Revenue Cycle Management at Bridge, a healthcare platform that helps providers get credentialed, enrolled with payers and paid. Zack and Megan cover payer contracting, superbills, out-of-network claims, eligibility limits, guaranteed payment and onboarding providers in 45 days.

item.title: [Understanding Healthcare with Zack Kanter] Credentialing explained with Varun Krishnamurthy at Assured Health
item.description:
WHY YOU: An AI-native credentialing and enrollment company's CEO on how insurers verify providers, where the bottlenecks and closed panels really are, and when outsourcing credentialing makes sense: the build-vs-buy and pricing logic for a step that gates every new provider you add.
Varun Krishnamurthy is the co-founder and CEO of Assured Health, an AI-powered provider credentialing and enrollment company. He and Zack cover how insurers verify providers, credentialing bottlenecks, closed panels, and when outsourcing credentialing makes sense.

item.title: [Vital Signs with Jacob Effron and Nikhil Krishnan] Ep 67: Abridge Leaders on AI-Native Healthcare, Doctors Who Code, and the Future of Clinical AI
item.description:
WHY YOU: Pairs with the Abridge sales-engine episode already in your feed: how an AI-native health company is run internally (15:59), where admin AI vs. clinical AI will actually make money (21:08), and Abridge's move into payers and prior auth (24:47). Abridge's CEO and a clinical scientist on AI-native company operations, doctors who code, prototypes vs production, regulation and partnerships, admin vs clinical AI, payers and prior authorization, and pre-visit workflows and triage. item.title: [The GTMnow Podcast] Legora's CRO: $3.5M to $200M+ ARR, the Fastest Direct Sales Motion | Patrick Forquer
item.description:
WHY YOU: The sales-side mechanics behind the legal-AI company you track, from the CRO who took Legora from $3.5M to $200M ARR: a pilot designed so customers keep what they build (24:00), hiring 2-to-1 post-sale and the forward-deploy structure (15:30), time-to-value as the leading indicator of revenue (18:30), and the shift to consumption pricing (56:00). Legora grew from $3.5M to more than $100M in revenue in roughly a year, which the show calls the fastest a direct-sales motion has gone from zero to $100M, then doubled in under six months to $200M ARR. Patrick Forquer spent seven years at Braze, from its early days through the IPO, before joining Legora, a vertical legal-AI company backed by Benchmark and Redpoint, when it was at $3.5M in revenue. He walks through that scaling journey: his three criteria for joining a company (founder, product, investors), why time-to-value is the number-one leading indicator of revenue, the pilot design that lets customers keep what they build, forward-deployed team structure, the Jude Law and Aaron Judge brand campaigns and how brand ROI was measured, the '8 Mile' approach to competitive objections, screening sales hires for AI fluency, and the move to consumption pricing. item.title: [The a16z Show] OpenAI: When AI Agents Use Computers Faster Than You [wildcard]
item.description:
WHY YOU: Every RCM and prior-auth workflow you evaluate ends up in a payer portal or EHR screen with no API. OpenAI's computer-use team on why agents that drive software through the screen are now at a scaling point, how they are being put against legacy ERP-style systems, why the harness around the model matters more than the model, and the deterministic guardrails enterprises set around them. Lab-side and a16z-hosted, so no pricing numbers; a wildcard for the mechanics behind the next generation of back-office agents.
OpenAI's Ari Weinstein and James Sun argue that computer-use agents, which operate software without APIs, are entering a scaling phase. They join a16z's Seema Amble and Fabrizio Serafini to discuss agents working with legacy ERP systems, why the harness around a model matters, and how enterprises can set deterministic guardrails. They also look ahead to agents that work in the background and adapt to users rather than requiring users to adapt to them.

item.title: [Get Paid with Manny Medina] How Intercom's CFO Bet the Business on Outcome-Based Pricing
item.description:
WHY YOU: The CFO who actually signed off on Intercom's per-resolution pricing for Fin, on the parts that matter to you: why a simple outcome price beat a cleverer one, how he trades model sophistication against unit economics, and how seller comp was rebuilt so reps would push the AI plan without eroding margin. The finance-side view of outcome-based pricing that the founder interviews skip.
Episode 50 of Get Paid. Host Manny Medina talks with Dan Griggs, Chief Financial Officer of Intercom, about how outcome-based pricing changes the economics of AI agents, why simple pricing beats complex pricing, and the strategic decisions behind SaaS companies' shift to charging for AI-powered work. Covered: moving from perpetual licenses to subscriptions while managing debt covenants; why outcome-based pricing may be the most sustainable model for AI agents; balancing AI model sophistication against unit economics; leading with principles in uncharted markets; designing seller compensation that drives transformation without destroying margins. Griggs's background includes electrical engineering, finance rotations at AT&T and Nestle, scaling Rocket Fuel from pre-IPO to over $400M in revenue, and Sitecore under private-equity ownership; at Intercom he pioneered outcome-based pricing for AI agents.

item.title: [Lifers with Christina Farr] Healthcare runs a 1980s model in 2026 | Aaron Miri, Baptist Health
item.description:
WHY YOU: The buyer's side of every pitch you make: a health system's chief digital officer on which back-office roles AI has already stopped him hiring (no help-desk hire in 18 months), what it would take to get claims paid same-day, why payer friction and liability still slow deployment, and how a system decides what it will actually pay for clinical AI. Journalist-hosted, no sponsor on this one.
Christina Farr talks with Aaron Miri, executive VP and chief digital and innovation officer at Baptist Health, about how AI is changing the way health systems operate and where liability, privacy law and payer friction still slow it down. Miri says Baptist hasn't hired a help desk agent in more than 18 months and expects AI to affect future hiring more than current roles, and argues for a universal patient identifier, the 'primary key' healthcare AI lacks.
